architecture.mechanism: Sediment filter pore-size selection governs particulate load reaching the RO membrane, balancing pre-filtration of foulants against membrane flux and solute rejection, so that a moderately tight sediment cartridge reduces fouling and improves treated water quality without unnecessarily restrictive pressure drop.
architecture.intervention: Install a multi-stage pretreatment train ahead of the RO membranes using a graded sediment pre-filter (e.g., 5 µm followed by 3 µm or 1 µm cartridges) sized to the city's raw feed-water turbidity and solids, selected empirically to minimize silt and bio-foulant loading on the RO elements while preserving throughput and avoiding excessive pressure drop that would raise energy and replacement costs.
architecture.expected_effect: Reduced contaminant breakthrough and slower filter/membrane fouling in the municipal RO units, giving more stable TDS, pH, turbidity, and color output, longer intervals between cartridge and membrane replacements, and lower lifecycle cost and maintenance burden across distributed city installations.
architecture.falsification_test: Run side-by-side pilot trials at two representative city intake points for at least 8–12 weeks: one skid with the existing single-stage pre-filter and one skid with the graded 5 µm + 3 µm (or 1 µm) pre-filter stack feeding identical RO membranes. Measure feed and product TDS, pH, turbidity (NTU), and color (TCU) daily, log transmembrane pressure differential, and record cumulative permeate volume between cleanings. If the graded-pretreatment skid does not show a statistically significant reduction in fouling rate (lower ΔTMP slope) and equal-or-better permeate quality versus the baseline, the mechanism is falsified for these feed conditions and pore sizes.
